title: About
text:
Hi! I’m Jin Liu.
This blog shares my weekly work for AEDS 6400. Each post uses economic data to practice data acquisition, cleaning, analysis, and visualization.

title: Why Lower New-Home Prices Have Not Restored Affordability
text:
Buying a home depends on more than its advertised price. Most households borrow, so mortgage rates determine how much of the price becomes a monthly payment. Income growth and inflation also affect whether comparisons across years are meaningful. I ask: How have home prices and mortgage rates jointly changed the affordability of buying a typical new U.S. home since 2000?
This question matters to households deciding whether a home fits their budget and to policymakers trying to understand why affordability can remain weak even when prices stop rising.

title: Why Lower New-Home Prices Have Not Restored Affordability
text:
Buying a home depends on more than its advertised price. Most households borrow, so mortgage rates determine how much of the price becomes a monthly payment. Income growth and inflation also affect whether comparisons across years are meaningful. I ask: How have home prices and mortgage rates jointly changed the affordability of buying a typical new U.S. home since 2000?
This question matters to households deciding whether a home fits their budget and to policymakers trying to understand why affordability can remain weak even when prices stop rising.

title: Why Lower New-Home Prices Have Not Restored Affordability
text:
Data and method
I download four public series programmatically from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis’s FRED CSV endpoint: the median sales price of new houses (MSPUS), the 30-year fixed mortgage rate (MORTGAGE30US), the Consumer Price Index (CPIAUCSL), and median household income (MEHOINUSA646N). The underlying sources are the Census Bureau and HUD, Freddie Mac, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and the Census Bureau.
The series have different frequencies, so I calculate annual averages of quarterly home prices, weekly mortgage rates, and monthly CPI. Household income is already annual. I limit the analysis to 2000–2025, the latest complete year shared by all four series.
Two transformations make the comparison economically meaningful. First, I use CPI to express home prices in 2025 dollars. Second, I estimate the monthly principal-and-interest payment on the median-priced home, assuming a 20% down payment and a 30-year fixed mortgage. I divide that payment by median monthly household income. This payment burden is an illustration, not a lending standard, and excludes property taxes, insurance, maintenance, and transaction costs. The complete R analysis downloads the data and generates every result.

title: Why Lower New-Home Prices Have Not Restored Affordability
section: Sticker prices overstate part of the long-run increase
text:
Sticker prices overstate part of the long-run increase









The nominal median new-home price increased from $167,550 in 2000 to $415,400 in 2025. After accounting for inflation, the increase is smaller: the 2000 price equals about $313,283 in 2025 dollars. Inflation therefore explains an important part of the apparent increase, although real home prices still rose by 33%.
The real-price series also changes the interpretation of the recent decline. In 2025 dollars, the annual average fell from approximately $476,353 in 2022 to $415,400 in 2025, a decline of 13%. Even after that correction, the 2025 level remained 3% above 2019. Buyers therefore received some price relief after 2022, but did not return to the pre-pandemic market.

title: Why Lower New-Home Prices Have Not Restored Affordability
text:
Mortgage rates reversed direction after 2021









The average 30-year mortgage rate fell to 3.0% in 2021, allowing buyers to finance expensive homes relatively cheaply. By 2025, the average was 6.6%. The higher rate matters because it raises every monthly payment without changing the home’s purchase price or providing the buyer with more housing.
High mortgage rates are not historically unique: the 2000 average was 8.1%. What changed is the amount being financed relative to income. The median new-home price equaled about 4.0 years of median household income in 2000 and 4.7 years in 2025. The same interest rate can therefore create a different burden when the loan principal and household income have changed.

title: Why Lower New-Home Prices Have Not Restored Affordability
section: The combined payment burden tells the clearest story
text:
The combined payment burden tells the clearest story









For the assumptions used here, the estimated payment rose from $1,285 per month in 2021 to $2,121 in 2025. It increased from 21.8% to 29.1% of median gross household income. The burden peaked at 33.1% in 2023.
The counterfactual line holds the mortgage rate at its 2021 average while allowing home prices and income to change. At that low rate, the 2025 payment would have been approximately $1,394, or 19.1% of income. The difference—about $728 per month—shows why modest price declines have not fully restored affordability.

title: Why Lower New-Home Prices Have Not Restored Affordability
text:
What this benchmark leaves out
This national comparison does not represent every buyer. MSPUS covers newly built homes, which can differ from existing homes in size, location, and quality. The median home and median household also come from separate datasets, so this is not the payment made by one observed household. Annual averages conceal changes within a year and large differences across local markets. Finally, many buyers put down less than 20%, and the calculation excludes mortgage insurance, property taxes, homeowners insurance, maintenance, fees, and closing costs. These omissions generally make the displayed payment smaller than the full monthly cost of ownership.

title: Why Lower New-Home Prices Have Not Restored Affordability
text:
Takeaway
New-home prices remain high, but the recent affordability squeeze cannot be understood from prices alone. The transition from a 3.0% mortgage rate in 2021 to 6.6% in 2025 added roughly $728 to the illustrative monthly payment on a 2025 median-priced new home. Households should evaluate homes using payment-to-income calculations, while durable policy improvements require attention to both financing conditions and the supply of homes.

title: Why Lower New-Home Prices Have Not Restored Affordability

title: Which Tech Skills Should I Learn? Evidence from Arbeitnow Jobs
text: Learning a new tool takes time. For someone interested in a software, data, or IT job, should the next project use Python, TypeScript, a cloud platform, or something else? Does the board offer remote or entry-level opportunities? Job advertisements offer practical clues. I used Arbeitnow, a Germany-focused job board, to examine skills, role types, work arrangement, and experience level.

title: Which Tech Skills Should I Learn? Evidence from Arbeitnow Jobs
text: Learning a new tool takes time. For someone interested in a software, data, or IT job, should the next project use Python, TypeScript, a cloud platform, or something else? Does the board offer remote or entry-level opportunities? Job advertisements offer practical clues. I used Arbeitnow, a Germany-focused job board, to examine skills, role types, work arrangement, and experience level.

title: Which Tech Skills Should I Learn? Evidence from Arbeitnow Jobs
section: From public pages to clean data
text:
From public pages to clean data
On September 21, 2026, my R collection script used rvest to read 100 public listing pages. It saved their HTML and extracted 5000 unique job titles and URLs. Of those titles, 1019 matched a documented software, data, or IT role pattern. Arbeitnow also offers a public job-board API with full descriptions; collecting its paginated feed avoided requesting thousands of individual job pages. The API ended after 29 pages of jobs and supplied 3153 unique descriptions, of which 543 matched the technology-role pattern. 1836 API jobs also appeared in the 100-page HTML snapshot. The two sources are snapshots of the same changing board, so their page lists do not line up exactly.


Code
library(rvest)
page <- read_html("data/raw/html/page-001.html")
links <- html_elements(page, "a[data-job-item-link]")
job_urls <- html_attr(links, "href")
job_titles <- html_text2(links)


The API pagination helper manages the paced feed requests. The separate analysis script cleans description HTML, removes duplicate URLs, and searches for 20 named technologies. It counts a skill once per job even when the word appears repeatedly. Every skill percentage below divides by the 543 technology jobs with descriptions, not by all HTML listings. The scripts save the cleaned data, tables, and figures; the README gives replication commands. The complete project is in the GitHub repository. Collection used sequential requests with pauses, followed the site’s robots.txt, and used no login or access workaround. Arbeitnow’s API terms ask users to link back to the site.

title: Which Tech Skills Should I Learn? Evidence from Arbeitnow Jobs
text:
Work arrangement and experience level
Only 42 of the 543 technology jobs (7.7%) are marked remote. The other 501 have remote = FALSE in the source. That means not marked remote; it does not prove they require full-time office attendance. Remote shares are 9.9% for infrastructure and security, 7.4% for software development, and 3.5% for data and machine learning. The last figure comes from just 2 remote postings, so I would not infer a stable difference between fields.



Bar chart of the percentage of each technology role group marked remote in the Arbeitnow API.


Experience is another constraint: 198 postings (36.5%) include a senior or lead term in the title, while only 41 (7.6%) include an early-career term. The rest do not state a clear level in the title. An entry-level or remote job seeker should therefore filter listings by those needs before using the overall skill ranking to plan a project.

title: Which Tech Skills Should I Learn? Evidence from Arbeitnow Jobs
section: What should a job seeker do?
text:
What should a job seeker do?
If I were targeting data or machine-learning roles, I would build a Python project that queries and analyzes data with SQL: those two skills appear in 49 of 57 data postings and 32 of them, respectively. For software development, I would show Python or TypeScript in a working application. For infrastructure, I would demonstrate deploying and monitoring an application with Kubernetes or a cloud service. These projects provide evidence of ability rather than a list of keywords on a résumé.
The sample has limits. Arbeitnow is one board, many jobs are Germany-focused, and the title filter may miss relevant roles. A technology mentioned in company background or as a preference is still counted. Only 378 of the 543 technology postings mention one of my 20 chosen terms, so the dictionary is incomplete. This analysis measures current advertised language, not hiring outcomes or the return to learning a skill.

title: Which Tech Skills Should I Learn? Evidence from Arbeitnow Jobs
text:
Takeaway
The useful lesson is to choose a role and work arrangement first, then use job descriptions to prioritize a small, demonstrable set of skills. Python is the broadest starting point here, but SQL, TypeScript, and Kubernetes matter differently across roles. Remote and early-career openings are a small, specifically labeled part of this sample. Check target postings before investing in a course, and repeat the analysis as listings change.

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Directions That Stay on Track
text:
Imagine drawing arrows on a stretchy sheet. You pull the sheet so that the arrows change length and tilt. Most arrows now point along different lines. But a few special arrows may stay on their original lines, even as they stretch.
Those special arrows capture the idea of eigenvectors. Their eigenvalues tell us how much they are scaled.
The names sound abstract because we often meet them through an equation before seeing the question they answer: Are there directions in which a complicated transformation acts like simple multiplication?

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Directions That Stay on Track
text:
Imagine drawing arrows on a stretchy sheet. You pull the sheet so that the arrows change length and tilt. Most arrows now point along different lines. But a few special arrows may stay on their original lines, even as they stretch.
Those special arrows capture the idea of eigenvectors. Their eigenvalues tell us how much they are scaled.
The names sound abstract because we often meet them through an equation before seeing the question they answer: Are there directions in which a complicated transformation acts like simple multiplication?

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Directions That Stay on Track
section: Think of a matrix as a rule for moving arrows
text:
Think of a matrix as a rule for moving arrows
A vector is an arrow described by its coordinates. For example, \((1,0)\) points one unit right, while \((1,1)\) points one unit right and one unit up.
A matrix can describe a linear transformation: a rule that preserves vector addition and multiplication by numbers. It can stretch, rotate, reflect, or shear arrows while keeping the origin fixed.
Consider this particular rule:
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
A\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2x+y\\x+2y\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The entries are instructions: double the first coordinate and add the second; then add the first coordinate to twice the second.
An arrow pointing right, \((1,0)\), becomes \((2,1)\). It now tilts upward. The transformation changed both its length and its direction.
But try an arrow pointing diagonally northeast:
\[
A\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}3\\3\end{pmatrix}
=3\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This arrow gets three times as long but stays on the same line. Therefore, \((1,1)\) is an eigenvector, with eigenvalue 3.
Now try the other diagonal:
\[
A\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This arrow stays exactly where it was. It is also an eigenvector, with eigenvalue 1.

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Directions That Stay on Track
text:
See the difference
The figure applies the same matrix to three arrows. Dashed arrows show the starting vectors; solid arrows show their transformed versions. Only the last two remain on their original lines.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

A = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])
vectors = [np.array([1, 0]), np.array([1, 1]), np.array([1, -1])]
titles = ["Ordinary direction", "Eigenvector: eigenvalue 3", "Eigenvector: eigenvalue 1"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4.6))

for ax, v, title in zip(axes, vectors, titles):
    result = A @ v
    t = np.linspace(-1.5, 3.5, 100)
    ax.plot(t * v[0], t * v[1], color="#dddddd", linewidth=1.5)
    ax.annotate("", xy=result, xytext=(0, 0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#C65319", lw=3))
    ax.annotate("", xy=v, xytext=(0, 0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#245A81", lw=2,
                                linestyle="--"))
    ax.axhline(0, color="#999999", lw=0.7)
    ax.axvline(0, color="#999999", lw=0.7)
    ax.set(xlim=(-1.5, 3.5), ylim=(-1.5, 3.5),
           xlabel="First coordinate", ylabel="Second coordinate", title=title)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.15)

fig.legend(handles=[Line2D([0], [0], color="#245A81", lw=2,
                          linestyle="--", label="Original vector"),
                    Line2D([0], [0], color="#C65319", lw=3,
                          label="Transformed vector")],
           loc="lower center", ncol=2, frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.09, 1, 1])
plt.show()








Figure 1: One transformation, three starting arrows. The horizontal arrow changes direction; the two diagonal eigenvectors stay on their original lines. In the right panel, the unchanged solid arrow overlaps the dashed original.

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Directions That Stay on Track
section: The equation is just a comparison
text:
The equation is just a comparison
The formal definition is short:
\[
A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{v}\ne\mathbf{0}.
\]
The left side says “apply the matrix.” The right side says “multiply the original vector by a single number.” An eigenvector is a nonzero vector for which those two operations give the same result. That number, \(\lambda\) (the Greek letter lambda), is the eigenvalue. MIT’s introduction to eigenvalues and eigenvectors
The sign and size matter:



Eigenvalue
What happens to the eigenvector?




\(3\)
Its length triples.


\(1\)
It stays unchanged.


\(0.5\)
Its length halves.


\(-2\)
Its length doubles and it points the opposite way.


\(0\)
It collapses to the zero vector.



So “never changes direction” needs a qualification: a negative eigenvalue reverses the arrow, and zero removes its direction entirely. The transformed vector remains on the original line. Also, an eigenvector is not unique in length: \((2,2)\) works just as well as \((1,1)\) in our example.

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Directions That Stay on Track
text:
Why this initially feels unintuitive
We usually describe this matrix using horizontal and vertical coordinates. From that viewpoint, it mixes the coordinates together. It seems natural to assume that mixing is unavoidable.
But our example becomes simpler when we use the two diagonal directions instead. Along one diagonal, the rule is “multiply by three.” Along the other, it is “multiply by one.”
Even the ordinary arrow can be broken into those two pieces:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}
=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
+\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Apply the transformation repeatedly. After \(n\) applications, the first piece has been multiplied by \(3^n\), while the second is unchanged:
\[
A^n\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}
=\frac{3^n}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
+\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The first piece eventually dwarfs the second, so the resulting arrow points increasingly close to the northeast diagonal. The eigenvectors explain the patterns; the eigenvalues explain how those patterns evolve.
This convenient decomposition works here because the two eigenvectors span the plane. Not every matrix has enough independent eigenvectors for this approach. A 90-degree rotation in the real plane, for example, leaves no nonzero arrow on its original line, so it has no real eigenvectors. MIT lecture notes

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Directions That Stay on Track
text:
An economic interpretation
As a deliberately simplified model, imagine that the two coordinates represent deviations in activity in two sectors. Let our matrix describe how those deviations propagate in one period. These numbers are illustrative assumptions, not estimates from economic data.
The vector \((1,1)\) represents both sectors moving together. Under this rule, that common movement triples each period. The vector \((1,-1)\) represents one sector rising while the other falls by the same amount. That difference remains unchanged.
Instead of tracking two interacting coordinates, we can track a common movement and an opposing movement. In this toy model, common shocks amplify, while opposing shocks persist. Actual economic conclusions would depend on whether the chosen rule fits the economy, but the mathematical benefit is already visible.

title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Directions That Stay on Track
text:
The takeaway
Eigenvectors identify directions where a linear transformation reduces to scaling. Eigenvalues tell us the scale factor, including whether the arrow reverses or disappears.
The surprising part is that a rule that mixes coordinates can become simple when viewed along the right directions. The next time you see \(A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}\), picture an arrow staying on its line—and ask how much it stretches.

title: Why Lower Rent Does Not Always Mean Less Housing Pressure
text:
Chester County’s median monthly rent was $1,763. In Centre County, it was $1,207. Yet renters in Centre were more likely to spend at least 30% of their income on rent. The county with the smaller bill had the higher burden.
A lower rent may look attractive, but how far it goes depends on the income available to pay it. For local housing organizations, focusing only on expensive areas could also miss renters struggling elsewhere.
Do Pennsylvania counties with lower rents generally have fewer renters spending a large share of their income on housing? I compare all 67 counties to answer that question. The aim is to see how much the price of housing tells us, and what we miss when we stop there.

title: Why Lower Rent Does Not Always Mean Less Housing Pressure
text:
Chester County’s median monthly rent was $1,763. In Centre County, it was $1,207. Yet renters in Centre were more likely to spend at least 30% of their income on rent. The county with the smaller bill had the higher burden.
A lower rent may look attractive, but how far it goes depends on the income available to pay it. For local housing organizations, focusing only on expensive areas could also miss renters struggling elsewhere.
Do Pennsylvania counties with lower rents generally have fewer renters spending a large share of their income on housing? I compare all 67 counties to answer that question. The aim is to see how much the price of housing tells us, and what we miss when we stop there.

title: Why Lower Rent Does Not Always Mean Less Housing Pressure
section: From Census tables to county maps
text:
From Census tables to county maps
I use the 2020–2024 American Community Survey, which combines five years of survey data. These are estimates for that period, not current apartment listings. The rent measure is median gross rent: the middle monthly rent, including utilities paid separately by the tenant, expressed in 2024 dollars.
For affordability, I calculate the share of rent-paying households spending 30% or more of their income on rent and utilities. I call this the rent-burden rate. Households whose ratio cannot be calculated are excluded. Across Pennsylvania, 48.2% of households with a calculable ratio met that threshold, and 24.9% spent at least half their income on rent.
The R scripts download the official tables and match each county to its Census map boundary. The statewide shares combine household counts; they are not simple averages of county rates. The data and methods notes explain the calculations and how to reproduce the analysis.

title: Why Lower Rent Does Not Always Mean Less Housing Pressure
text:
Where rents are higher






Figure 1: Median monthly gross rent by Pennsylvania county, 2020–2024. Selected counties are labeled for comparison.



Higher rents cluster in the southeast. Chester’s median is $1,763, compared with $1,397 in Philadelphia. Much of western and central Pennsylvania has lower rents. Bedford’s median is $784, while Allegheny’s is $1,153.
The first map shows where rents are higher. The next asks whether those are also the places where renters have the most trouble paying them.

title: Why Lower Rent Does Not Always Mean Less Housing Pressure
section: Housing pressure reaches beyond expensive counties
text:
Housing pressure reaches beyond expensive counties






Figure 2: Share of rent-paying households spending at least 30% of income on rent. Open circles mark counties with larger margins of error.



Housing pressure is not confined to the highest-rent counties in the southeast. Centre, in central Pennsylvania, has a burden rate of 57.0%. Monroe, in the northeast, is at 57.0%. Both have lower median rents than Chester, where the rate is 47.8%.
The contrast also appears closer to Philadelphia. Its rent is below Chester’s, but its burden rate is higher, at 52.3%. Farther west, Bedford combines a much lower rent with an estimated burden rate of 49.9%. Bedford’s estimate has a wider margin of error, so small differences between it and other counties should not be treated as firm rankings.
Taken together, the maps show that high rents and heavy rent burdens do not line up neatly. Chester, Montgomery and Bucks, the three highest-rent counties, are all in the southeast, but their burden rates are 47.8%, 49.0% and 47.9% respectively, below Centre and Monroe. In western Pennsylvania, Lawrence has a median rent of just $831, yet an estimated 51.0% of renters meet the burden threshold. Housing pressure reaches beyond the most expensive areas; the income comparison below helps explain why.

title: Why Lower Rent Does Not Always Mean Less Housing Pressure
section: What happens when we compare every county?
text:
What happens when we compare every county?






Figure 3: Median rent and rent-burden rate for all 67 counties. Vertical bars show approximate 90% margins of error for burden rates.



The broader pattern is still clear: higher-rent counties generally have higher burden rates. The correlation is 0.54, counting each county equally. The relationship is positive, but there is plenty of variation around it.
Centre and Chester illustrate that variation. Allegheny offers another comparison: its rent is close to Centre’s, while its burden rate is lower, at 46.2%. Lower rents often go with lighter burdens, but rent alone does not tell us which county has a larger share of struggling renters.

title: Why Lower Rent Does Not Always Mean Less Housing Pressure
text:
Income helps explain the difference
To see why the maps differ, I added median renter household income from ACS table B25119. Centre’s median renter income is $39,074 a year, compared with $72,048 in Chester. Centre’s rent is lower, but its renter income is lower by much more.
Dividing annual median rent by median renter income gives 37.1% for Centre and 29.4% for Chester. Monroe’s renter income is $47,645, putting its ratio at 35.1%. These comparisons help explain why housing pressure extends beyond the high-rent southeast: a smaller rent bill can still be large relative to local renters’ incomes.






Figure 4: Annual median rent divided by median renter income, compared with the actual rent-burden rate. Each point represents one county.



Across the 67 counties, this income-based comparison has a correlation of 0.88 with the burden rate, compared with 0.54 for rent alone. This is a ratio of two county medians, not the share of income paid by a typical household. The stronger relationship is also partly expected: both measures compare housing costs with income. It helps us read the maps, rather than proving what causes a county’s burden rate.
Centre has an important local feature: Penn State’s University Park campus. The county’s 2023 Housing Needs Assessment links high burden among its lowest-income renters to the concentration of college students. It also notes that resources such as student loans can complicate comparisons based on reported income. Students are therefore a plausible part of Centre’s story, although these county totals cannot separate their contribution from that of other renters. Households with zero or negative income have noncomputable ratios and are excluded from my burden rate; they are not automatically counted as burdened.

title: Why Lower Rent Does Not Always Mean Less Housing Pressure
section: What should a renter take from this?
text:
What should a renter take from this?
When comparing places to live, I would start with actual rent and utility costs, then compare them with the income I expected to have there. A county with cheaper housing may also offer lower earnings. For local housing organizations, the two maps together identify places worth examining more closely, including lower-rent counties where many households still struggle.
The ACS estimates cover 2020–2024, not today’s listings, and county figures hide differences between neighborhoods and households. Error bars show uncertainty in the burden estimates; map circles flag margins above five percentage points. The rent measures exclude households paying no cash rent, while the added income measure covers all renter households. The 30% threshold offers a common comparison, but does not account for every household’s other expenses.

title: Why Lower Rent Does Not Always Mean Less Housing Pressure
text:
Takeaway
Lower rents generally go with lower rent burdens in Pennsylvania, but Centre and Lawrence show why price alone can mislead. Rent tells us what housing costs; renter income helps explain how hard it is to pay. Renters should compare costs with their own expected income. Housing organizations should examine low renter incomes alongside high rents when deciding where to look more closely at housing needs.

title: Does Education Protect Workers from Unemployment?
text: Unemployment is costly for workers and families, but its burden is not distributed evenly. Education may reduce unemployment risk by giving workers more specialized skills, access to a wider range of occupations, or stronger attachment to employers. It may also separate workers into industries that respond differently to recessions. I ask: How does unemployment vary by education among U.S. adults ages 25-64, and does the gap change when the labor market weakens?

title: Does Education Protect Workers from Unemployment?
text: Unemployment is costly for workers and families, but its burden is not distributed evenly. Education may reduce unemployment risk by giving workers more specialized skills, access to a wider range of occupations, or stronger attachment to employers. It may also separate workers into industries that respond differently to recessions. I ask: How does unemployment vary by education among U.S. adults ages 25-64, and does the gap change when the labor market weakens?

title: Does Education Protect Workers from Unemployment?
text:
Data and method
I use IPUMS CPS, which harmonizes the monthly Current Population Survey across time. My extract contains April Basic Monthly samples from 2000 through 2025 and the variables YEAR, MONTH, AGE, EDUC, LABFORCE, EMPSTAT, and WTFINL. April gives one comparable cross-section per year and captures the abrupt pandemic disruption in April 2020.
The analysis includes civilians ages 25-64 who are in the labor force. I group education into four levels: less than high school, high school or GED, some college or an associate degree, and a bachelor’s degree or higher. A person is unemployed when the detailed EMPSTAT code is 20-22. The unemployment rate is unemployed people divided by the civilian labor force.
Every estimate uses the final Basic Monthly CPS person weight, WTFINL:
\[
\text{Unemployment rate}_g=
\frac{\sum_{i\in g} WTFINL_i\times Unemployed_i}
{\sum_{i\in g} WTFINL_i}.
\]
This makes the results describe the U.S. population represented by the CPS rather than the raw observations in the extract. The complete analysis script generates every table and figure.

title: Does Education Protect Workers from Unemployment?
text:
A persistent education gradient

The first figure establishes whether unemployment rates differ consistently across education groups and shows how all four groups move with the national labor market. Comparing 2000, 2010, 2020, and 2025 also reveals which groups experienced the largest increases during weak labor markets.
In April 2025, the weighted unemployment rate was 6.3% for workers without a high-school diploma and 2.4% for workers with a bachelor’s degree or higher. The same ordering is visible across most years. During the April 2020 shock, the rates rose to 20.8% and 7.9%, respectively. Education therefore marks a persistent difference in unemployment risk, while all groups still move with the wider economy.

title: Does Education Protect Workers from Unemployment?
section: The gap changes over the business cycle
text:
The gap changes over the business cycle

The second figure subtracts the unemployment rate for bachelor’s-degree holders from each other group’s rate. This shifts attention from the overall cycle to inequality in unemployment risk. Higher lines during 2010 or 2020 indicate that downturns widened the education gap rather than raising unemployment equally for everyone.
The gap between the least-educated group and bachelor’s-degree holders was 12.9 percentage points in April 2020, compared with 3.9 percentage points in April 2025. The recession-era gap was therefore larger. This comparison shows whether weaker labor markets merely raise unemployment or also concentrate more of the increase among workers with less education.

title: Does Education Protect Workers from Unemployment?
section: Education is not simply standing in for age
text:
Education is not simply standing in for age

Education and age are related: older adults have had more time to complete degrees, while younger workers have less labor-market experience. The final figure compares education groups within four age bands in 2025. A consistent education gradient within rows would show that the overall relationship is not solely the result of different age composition.
In 4 of the four age groups, unemployment was higher for adults without a high-school diploma than for adults with a bachelor’s degree or higher. The comparison does not remove every possible difference between workers, but it shows how much of the aggregate education pattern remains after making a simple age adjustment.

title: Does Education Protect Workers from Unemployment?
text:
Interpretation and takeaway
These figures describe associations, not causal effects. Degree holders differ from other workers in occupation, industry, location, experience, and many other ways. The analysis also uses one month per year, so it describes April conditions rather than an annual average.
The practical lesson is that a single national unemployment rate can conceal large differences in economic security. Read together, the figures show whether more-educated workers experience lower unemployment in ordinary years, whether their advantage expands in downturns, and whether it remains visible within age groups. The main takeaway is that education is related both to the level of unemployment risk and to how strongly workers are exposed when the labor market deteriorates. For workforce agencies, the descriptive evidence can help target job-search assistance and retraining toward less-educated workers, especially during downturns.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Would I reach the same conclusion about economic mobility if I measured someone’s earnings at 27 instead of 37? Someone in their twenties may still be finishing school or changing jobs. Their earnings may say more about that stage of life than their longer-run position. This matters when using mobility estimates to judge how family background shapes opportunity.
I use Python and SQL to match mothers with their adult children, then ask how the estimated earnings relationship changes when I average several years or measure the children later.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Would I reach the same conclusion about economic mobility if I measured someone’s earnings at 27 instead of 37? Someone in their twenties may still be finishing school or changing jobs. Their earnings may say more about that stage of life than their longer-run position. This matters when using mobility estimates to judge how family background shapes opportunity.
I use Python and SQL to match mothers with their adult children, then ask how the estimated earnings relationship changes when I average several years or measure the children later.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Start with people, then income
I use the public NLSY79 and Child/Young Adult files covering 1979–2018. The child file provides a mother’s ID, which connects to her record in NLSY79. The original files contain 11,545 children; every child has a matching mother.
Here, “income” means annual earnings from wages, salaries, commissions and tips, rather than total household resources. I convert amounts to 2018 dollars using the BLS Consumer Price Index. Negative survey codes mean missing information; a reported zero is a real observation.
To follow along, install the dependencies and run the scripts from this post’s folder:
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python code/analyze.py
python code/plot.py
The repository includes compact extracts, so downloading the large originals is optional. The README explains both routes, the variable names and the income reference years.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
section: Match the two generations with SQL
text:
Match the two generations with SQL
The first script creates a SQLite database. Open it in Python and match the IDs:
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

con = sqlite3.connect("data/analysis.sqlite")
matched = pd.read_sql_query("""
    SELECT c.child_id, c.mother_id
    FROM children AS c
    JOIN mothers AS m ON c.mother_id = m.mother_id
    WHERE m.sex = 2
""", con)
SELECT chooses the columns to return. JOIN connects records with the same mother ID; it does not match people by row order. Several children can share one mother, so the matched table keeps one row per child.
The IDs tell me who belongs to which family. Next, I need an earnings measure for each person. Instead of letting one unusually good or bad year represent a mother’s earnings, I average her available observations between ages 30 and 44:
mother_average = pd.read_sql_query("""
    SELECT person_id AS mother_id,
           AVG(wage_real) AS mother_mean,
           COUNT(*) AS mother_n
    FROM earnings
    WHERE cohort = 'mother' AND age BETWEEN 30 AND 44
    GROUP BY person_id
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 AND AVG(wage_real) > 0
""", con)
WHERE selects the relevant records. GROUP BY gathers each mother’s years together. AVG and COUNT are aggregations: they produce her average earnings and number of observations. HAVING keeps groups with at least three valid years and a positive average. Average the dollar amounts first, then take logs.
The script repeats this step for children at ages 25–34 and joins both averages back to the matched IDs. Zeros remain in these averages. For the single-year comparison, it selects the valid observation nearest age 37 for mothers and 30 for children, choosing the earlier year in a tie. Pairs with zero selected earnings are excluded because their logarithms are undefined; both estimates then use exactly the same pairs.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
One year versus several years
An intergenerational earnings elasticity, or IGE, is the slope from regressing log child earnings on log maternal earnings. An elasticity of 0.10 means that 10% higher maternal earnings are associated with approximately 1% higher child earnings. It describes an association, not a causal effect.
import numpy as np

pairs = pd.read_csv("data/matched_averaging.csv")
x = np.log(pairs["mother_mean"])
y = np.log(pairs["child_mean"])
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
intercept, ige = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
Use mother_one and child_one to estimate the single-year version. The script clusters uncertainty by mother because siblings share a family.



Using the same pairs, the estimated elasticity is higher with several years of earnings. Bars show 95% confidence intervals.


With one year of earnings, the estimated relationship is about half as strong as with several years (48%). The families have not changed; the way I measure their earnings has. Among 2,114 pairs, the estimate rises from 0.055 to 0.113.
A year of unemployment, changing hours or a bonus can shift someone’s earnings. Averaging reduces the influence of these temporary changes and can better reflect their longer-run position. The typical pair contributes 9 maternal years and 3 child years. These estimates describe mothers’ own earnings, which capture only part of a family’s resources; they should not be read as estimates of overall family-income mobility.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Measuring later in a career
Averaging and choosing an age address different problems. Several early-career years can still give an incomplete picture of later earnings. This is life-cycle bias: earnings measured at one age need not reflect the relationship between the generations’ lifetime earnings.
Someone who stays in education may earn little at first and more later. If earnings paths differ across family backgrounds, averaging early earnings alone will not fix the timing problem.
For this check, I hold maternal average earnings fixed and select each child’s earnings nearest ages 27 and 37, within ages 25–29 and 35–39. The same 1,004 children appear in both estimates. Interviews become less frequent after age 30, so this comparison uses one observation in each age window.



The estimate is higher when these same children’s earnings are measured later, but the difference remains uncertain.


The estimate is higher when I measure the same children later, rising from 0.088 to 0.129. But the difference is uncertain: its 95% confidence interval runs from -0.020 to 0.103, including zero. This fits the idea that early-career earnings can miss part of the longer-run relationship, but this sample cannot say exactly how much.



Sample check
Children




Matched to mothers
11,545


Eligible averages in both generations
2,870


Positive single-year earnings in both generations
2,114


Positive earnings at both younger and older ages
1,004



These are unweighted estimates for selected wage earners, not all American families. The older children disproportionately come from mothers who gave birth young. Missing interviews, top-coded high earnings and the exclusion of zero single-year earnings also limit the comparison. Calendar year changes alongside age, and neither age window measures lifetime earnings.

title: Does One Year of Income Tell the Whole Story?
text:
Takeaway
Before comparing two mobility estimates, check how earnings were measured. In this sample, using several years produces a stronger mother–child earnings relationship than using one year. Measuring children later also raises the estimate, although that difference is less certain. The useful lesson is to look beyond the headline number: whose earnings, which ages, and how many years?

title: Finding Work After College: How Do Majors Compare?
text:
Does a high-paying major also make it easier to find work? In 2024, computer science graduates had median early-career wages of $87,000, but their unemployment rate was 7.0%. Nursing paid less, at $70,000, while its unemployment rate was 2.1%. If I looked only at salaries, I would miss that difference.
For someone choosing a major or preparing for graduation, the question is not just how much a job might pay. It is also whether graduates are working, and what kinds of jobs they hold. I use two interactive charts to explore the overall job market and then compare those measures across majors.

title: Finding Work After College: How Do Majors Compare?
text:

Nursing paid less, at $70,000, while its unemployment rate was 2.1%. If I looked only at salaries, I would miss that difference.
For someone choosing a major or preparing for graduation, the question is not just how much a job might pay. It is also whether graduates are working, and what kinds of jobs they hold. I use two interactive charts to explore the overall job market and then compare those measures across majors.

title: Finding Work After College: How Do Majors Compare?
section: How difficult is the job market?
text:
How difficult is the job market?
The New York Fed’s graduate labor-market data put the recent-graduate unemployment rate at 5.7% in June 2026, compared with 4.1% for all workers. Recent graduates here are ages 22–27 with at least a bachelor’s degree, excluding people still in school.

Figure 1. Unemployment rates through June 2026. Source: New York Fed, using CPS/IPUMS. Rates are seasonally adjusted and smoothed over three months; October 2025 is estimated by the source. All groups exclude current students.
Use the time menu or slider to explore a period, and click a legend label to hide a group. In January 1990, recent graduates’ unemployment rate was 3.4%, compared with 5.1% for all workers. By June 2026, it was 5.7% versus 4.1%. That reversal helps explain why graduation can feel less like a secure landing today.
The comparison with other young workers adds context. Among 22–27-year-olds without a bachelor’s degree, unemployment was 7.2% in June 2026, higher than among recent graduates. Graduates face a difficult market, but that does not mean their peers without degrees are doing better. Comparing people of similar ages also avoids treating the experience of older workers as the only benchmark.

title: Finding Work After College: How Do Majors Compare?
text:
Three ways to compare majors
For majors, I use the same source’s 2024 ACS-based data, covering 73 fields. These annual figures describe an earlier period than the monthly chart.
Unemployment measures the share of the labor force without work and looking for it. Underemployment measures the share of employed graduates in jobs that typically do not require a college degree. It does not mean their job is unrelated to their subject. Early-career wages are median annual wages for full-time workers ages 22–27 with a bachelor’s degree only, rather than starting salaries. The two employment rates include graduates with higher degrees as well; all measures exclude current students.

Figure 2. Outcomes by major, 2024. Source: New York Fed, using ACS/IPUMS. Dotted lines mark the published overall wage and unemployment benchmarks. Color shows underemployment; axes and the color scale stay fixed when filtering.
Hover over a point to identify its major and see all three measures. The first menu changes the comparison; the second highlights a particular major. If that major falls outside the filter, the message says so. This lets me explore individual fields without covering the chart in overlapping labels.

title: Finding Work After College: How Do Majors Compare?
section: What changes when I change the question?
text:
What changes when I change the question?
The published overall benchmarks are $58,000 for wages, 4.2% for unemployment and 39.4% for underemployment. These are reference points, not standards for a “good” major.
Selecting higher pay leaves 27 majors. Adding lower unemployment reduces that to 12. Computer science and computer engineering disappear: their high wages coexist with unemployment rates of 7.0% and 7.8%. Higher pay among full-time workers does not describe the experience of everyone seeking work.
The remaining group includes nursing, accounting, finance, economics and several engineering fields. Of these 12 majors, 11 also have below-overall underemployment. In this group, the three measures mostly point in the same direction.
The final filter asks a different question: which majors have lower unemployment but higher underemployment? It shows 17 fields. Agriculture has unemployment of 1.4%, yet underemployment of 57.1%. Criminal justice also falls into this group, with underemployment of 65.8%. Finding work and finding work that usually requires a degree are different outcomes. Switching filters makes that distinction visible.

title: Finding Work After College: How Do Majors Compare?
text:
What these comparisons leave out
These are group averages and medians, not predictions for an individual. They do not account for differences in students, locations or experience, and cannot show what changing majors would do to someone’s prospects. The files do not provide uncertainty intervals, so I would not read small gaps as firm rankings. They also do not measure how long a job search takes. A job classified as underemployment can still be worthwhile or a step toward another role.

title: Finding Work After College: How Do Majors Compare?
text:
Takeaway
Before calling a major promising, ask: promising in which way? A high salary, a low unemployment rate and a low underemployment rate answer different questions. I would use the chart to compare fields I am considering, then look more closely at the jobs and skills behind those numbers. It is a useful starting point for a career decision, rather than a reason to choose a subject from its salary alone.

title: Why Lower New-Home Prices Have Not Restored Affordability
section: What this means for households and policymakers
text:
What this means for households and policymakers
For a prospective buyer, the useful comparison is the complete monthly cost relative to income, rather than the listing price alone. In 2025, principal and interest on the typical new home consumed about 29.1% of median gross household income before taxes, insurance, or maintenance. Buyers should calculate the payment at the rate they can actually obtain and leave room for those additional costs.
For policymakers, the results separate two problems. Lower rates would reduce payments quickly, but rates move with broader financial conditions. Expanding housing supply addresses the price side more directly and can improve affordability without depending on a return to unusually low mortgage rates.
